lessons.title: From the Government of India Act 1935 & the Freedom Movement to the Constituent Assembly Debates (1946–1949)
lessons.levelTitle: Origins of the Indian Constitutional System (1935–1950)

sections.title: 1. Lesson Title & Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
* **Title:** From the Government of India Act 1935 & the Freedom Movement to the Constituent Assembly Debates (1946–1949)

* **Measurable Learning Outcomes:**
  1. Compare the two historical streams that shaped the Indian Constitution: (a) the **Colonial Institutional Stream** (specifically the `[🏛️ Government of India Act, 1935](/atlas/hist_goi_1935)`) and (b) the **Nationalist & Social-Reform Constitutional Stream** (Constitution of India Bill 1895, Nehru Report 1928, Karachi Resolution 1931, Sapru Committee Report 1945, and anti-caste struggles).
  2. Trace the formation, composition, and working method of the `[🏛️ Constituent Assembly of India](/atlas/hist_const_assembly)` (9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949), including the role of `[🏛️ Jawaharlal Nehru's Objectives Resolution](/atlas/hist_obj_resolution)`, Constitutional Adviser **Sir B.N. Rau**, and the `[🏛️ Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar](/atlas/hist_drafting_comm)`.
  3. Evaluate Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's defence in the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) of why borrowing and adapting administrative provisions from the 1935 Act was not "slavish imitation" but pragmatic state-building transformed by universal adult suffrage and Fundamental Rights.

sections.title: 3. Compelling Opening Question / Real-World Problem
sections.text:
> **The Accusation of "A Carbon Copy of the 1935 Act":**  
> On 4 November 1948, when Dr. B.R. Ambedkar rose in the Constituent Assembly to introduce the Draft Constitution, several critics inside the House complained: *"Over 200 articles of this Draft Constitution are lifted almost word-for-word from the British Government of India Act, 1935! Did we fight for freedom only to copy the colonial ruler's statute book?"*  
> **The Question:** Why did the framers retain the administrative skeleton of the `[🏛️ Government of India Act, 1935](/atlas/hist_goi_1935)` (three legislative lists, office of the Governor, Federal/Supreme Court, Public Service Commissions, emergency machinery) while simultaneously repealing the 1935 Act in `[📜 Article 395](/atlas/art_395)`? What fundamentally changed between 1935 and 1950 that turned an instrument of imperial control into a charter of democratic self-rule?

sections.title: 4. Beginner-Friendly Foundation (Before Advanced Terminology)
sections.text:
Imagine a town where a colonial railway station and track network were originally built to transport raw cotton to a port for an empire. After independence, the citizens do not tear up the steel railway tracks simply because the British laid them; instead, they **change who owns the railway, where the trains go, and who is allowed to board**—opening third-class and first-class coaches to every citizen equally and connecting rural villages to schools and hospitals.

That is exactly how the framers treated the institutional machinery of pre-1947 India:
* **What they kept and adapted (The Administrative Tracks):** Federal division of subjects into three lists (`[📜 Seventh Schedule](/atlas/sched_7)`), an integrated court system, a merit-based Public Service Commission (`[🏛️ UPSC](/atlas/inst_upsc)`), and audit by an independent `[🏛️ Comptroller and Auditor-General](/atlas/inst_cag)`.
* **What they revolutionized (The Engine & Moral Purpose):** Under the 1935 Act, barely $10\%–14\%$ of adults had the right to vote (based on property, tax, and education qualifications), the Viceroy and Governors held unchecked veto and "reserved" powers answerable only to London, and citizens had **zero enforceable Fundamental Rights**. The 1950 Constitution replaced imperial sovereignty with **Universal Adult Suffrage (`[📜 Article 326](/atlas/art_326)`)**, **Collective Cabinet Responsibility (`[📜 Article 75(3)](/atlas/art_75)`)**, and **Enforceable Fundamental Rights & Socio-Economic Directives (`[📜 Parts III & IV](/atlas/part_III)`)**.

sections.title: 5. Detailed Teachable Sections
sections.text:
#### Section 5.1: The Two Genealogies of the Indian Constitution
To understand why the Constitution of India looks the way it does, scholars (such as Granville Austin in *The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation*, 1966, and Rohit De) trace two intersecting historical streams:

| Historical Milestone | Year | Key Constitutional Contribution to the 1950 Text |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Constitution of India Bill (*Swaraj Bill*)** | 1895 | Inspired by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak; first indigenous constitutional text demanding free speech, inviolability of the citizen's home, equality before law, and free state education. |
| **2. Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford)** | 1919 | Introduced bicameralism at the Centre, Public Service Commission precursor, and provincial "dyarchy" (highlighting why divided executive accountability fails). |
| **3. Motilal Nehru Report** | 1928 | First comprehensive constitutional draft by Indian leaders: demanded 19 enforceable **Fundamental Rights** (including women's equal rights and freedom of conscience), parliamentary responsible government, and linguistic reorganization of provinces. |
| **4. Karachi Resolution on Fundamental Rights & Economic Policy** | 1931 | Drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru and presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel; fused civil-political liberties with **socio-economic obligations** (living wage, abolition of serfdom, protection of women and child workers)—the direct ancestor of `[📜 Part III](/atlas/part_III)` + `[📜 Part IV](/atlas/part_IV)`. |
| **5. Poona Pact & Anti-Caste Constitutionalism** | 1932 | Negotiated between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi; established the framework of **reserved seats in legislatures with joint electorates** (`[📜 Articles 330 & 332](/atlas/art_330)`) and constitutional commitments against untouchability. |
| **6. `[🏛️ Government of India Act, 1935](/atlas/hist_goi_1935)`** | 1935 | 321 Sections and 10 Schedules; supplied the structural blueprint for the `[📜 Seventh Schedule](/atlas/sched_7)` (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent Lists), Federal Court (`[🏛️ Supreme Court](/atlas/inst_supreme_court)`), Office of Governor (`[📜 Article 153](/atlas/art_153)`), and administrative relations (`[📜 Articles 256–257](/atlas/art_256)`). |
| **7. Sapru Committee Report** | 1945 | Chaired by Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru; explicitly recommended dividing rights into **Justiciable Fundamental Rights** (`[📜 Part III](/atlas/part_III)`) and **Non-Justiciable Directive Principles** (`[📜 Part IV](/atlas/part_IV)`). |

#### Section 5.2: Inside the Constituent Assembly (1946–1949) — How the Text Was Forged
Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of May 1946, the `[🏛️ Constituent Assembly](/atlas/hist_const_assembly)` held its first sitting on **9 December 1946** (with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary Chairman and **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** elected permanent President on 11 December 1946). Following the Mountbatten Plan and Partition (3 June 1947), the Assembly's membership for India stood at **299 members** (229 elected from British Indian Provincial Legislatures via proportional representation + 70 representing the Princely States).

How did 299 members produce the world's most detailed democratic constitution across **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** (11 sessions, 165 sitting days)? Through a four-stage deliberative architecture:
1. **Stage 1 — The Moral Compass (`[🏛️ Objectives Resolution](/atlas/hist_obj_resolution)`):** Moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on **13 December 1946** and unanimously adopted on **22 January 1947**, setting the foundational principles of popular sovereignty, federal autonomy, minority safeguards, and social/economic/political justice.
2. **Stage 2 — Subject Committees & Constitutional Adviser Sir B.N. Rau:** Major committees—including the *Union Powers Committee* and *Union Constitution Committee* (chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru), the *Provincial Constitution Committee* and *Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal/Excluded Areas* (chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with the *Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee* chaired by J.B. Kripalani and *Minorities Sub-Committee* by H.C. Mookherjee)—submitted reports. Using these reports and comparative research across 60+ global constitutions, Constitutional Adviser **Sir B.N. Rau** prepared the first **October 1947 Draft Constitution** (243 Articles and 13 Schedules).
3. **Stage 3 — `[🏛️ The Drafting Committee](/atlas/hist_drafting_comm)` (Appointed 29 August 1947):** Chaired by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** (alongside Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Dr. K.M. Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadulla, N. Madhava Rau, and T.T. Krishnamachari), the Committee scrutinized Rau's draft clause by clause, publishing the **February 1948 Draft Constitution** (315 Articles, 8 Schedules) for nationwide public comment for eight months.
4. **Stage 4 — Clause-by-Clause Public Debate & Amendment:** During the Second Reading (15 November 1948 to 17 October 1949), members tabled **7,635 amendments**, of which **2,473 were actually moved, debated, and voted on** line by line on the floor of the House! On **26 November 1949** (`[🏛️ Adoption 26 Nov 1949](/atlas/hist_adoption_1949)`), the Assembly adopted the final Constitution (395 Articles, 8 Schedules). Under `[📜 Article 394](/atlas/art_394)` (PDF p. 282), 15 transitional/citizenship/election articles came into force immediately on 26 November 1949, and the remaining provisions commenced on **26 January 1950** (chosen to honour the 26 January 1930 *Purna Swaraj* declaration).

sections.title: 6. Historical, Philosophical & Institutional Context
sections.text:
Responding to the charge that the Draft Constitution borrowed heavily from the 1935 Act and Western constitutions, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar gave a classic reply on **4 November 1948** (CAD Vol. VII, pp. 37–38):
> *"One likes to ask whether there can be anything new in a Constitution framed at this hour in the history of the world. More than hundred years have rolled over when the first written Constitution was drafted. It has been followed by many countries reducing their Constitutions to writing. What the scope of a Constitution should be has long been settled. Similarly what are the fundamentals of a Constitution are recognized all over the world. Given these facts, all Constitutions in their main provisions must look similar. The only new things, if there can be any, in a Constitution framed so late in the day are the variations made to remove the faults and to accommodate it to the needs of the country. The charge of producing a blind copy of the Constitutions of other countries is based, I am sure, on an inadequate study of the Constitution... As to the accusation that the Draft Constitution has produced a good part of the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, I make no apologies. There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing. It involves no plagiarism. Nobody holds any patent rights in the fundamental ideas of a Constitution. What I am sorry about is that the provisions taken from the Government of India Act, 1935, relate mostly to the details of administration."*

And why did Dr. Ambedkar include "details of administration" in the Constitution itself rather than leaving them to ordinary statutes? Because in a newly independent society where constitutional morality was still fragile, leaving the basic structure of administration to ordinary legislative majorities risked allowing a partisan majority to pervert administrative machinery without even amending the Constitution!

sections.title: 7. Everyday Indian Civic Examples & Analogies
sections.text: * **Why 26 November vs. 26 January Matters (`[📜 Article 394](/atlas/art_394)`):** Why did Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (Citizenship), Article 324 (Election Commission), and Articles 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393 come into force two months *early* on **26 November 1949** under Article 394 (PDF p. 282)? Because before the President could take oath and the Republic could officially commence on **26 January 1950**, India legally needed to know *who its citizens were* (`Arts. 5–9`) and needed the Election Commission (`Art. 324`) and provisional presidential election rules (`Art. 380`) already operational!

sections.title: 8. Verbatim Constitutional Articles & Primary Sources
sections.text:
* **Article 394, Part XXII (Official 2026 Constitution PDF, p. 282):**
  > **394. Commencement.—**This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.
* **Article 395, Part XXII (Official 2026 Constitution PDF, p. 283):**
  > **395. Repeals.—**The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

sections.title: 10. Common Misconceptions & Their Corrections
sections.text:
* **Misconception:** *"Dr. B.R. Ambedkar single-handedly wrote the first draft of the Constitution without prior committees or drafts."*
  * **Correction (historical evidence):** Constitutional Adviser **Sir B.N. Rau** prepared the initial October 1947 Draft Constitution synthesizing the reports of the Union Powers, Provincial Constitution, and Fundamental Rights/Minorities Committees (chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Patel). **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, as Chairman of the 7-member `[🏛️ Drafting Committee](/atlas/hist_drafting_comm)`, then re-architected, refined, and heroically piloted every single article through 114 days of intense clause-by-clause debate—earning T.T. Krishnamachari's tribute that a disproportionately heavy burden of the drafting work fell upon Dr. Ambedkar's shoulders.

sections.title: 12. Questions Requiring Active Reasoning
sections.text:
1. Why did the Sapru Committee (1945) and the Constituent Assembly divide rights into **Justiciable Fundamental Rights (`[📜 Part III](/atlas/part_III)`)** and **Non-Justiciable Directive Principles (`[📜 Part IV](/atlas/part_IV)`)** in 1949? If a newly independent country with massive fiscal scarcity in 1950 had made every socio-economic goal immediately enforceable by court decree on Day 1, what institutional crisis would have occurred?
2. Explain why Dr. Ambedkar argued that putting administrative details into the Constitution was necessary in a society where **constitutional morality** was not yet deeply ingrained.

sections.title: 13. Knowledge-Check Assessments with Explained Answers
sections.text:
* **Question 2.1.1:** Which historic resolution of the Indian National Congress in 1931 first combined civil-political Fundamental Rights with socio-economic duties of the State (such as a living wage and protection of labour)?
  * **A.** The Poona Pact, 1932.
  * **B.** The **Karachi Resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, 1931**. *(Correct)*
  * **C.** The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946.
  * **D.** The Mountbatten Plan, 1947.
  * **Explained Rationale:** Adopted at the March 1931 Karachi Session (drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru and presided over by Sardar Patel), the Karachi Resolution declared that *"in order to end the exploitation of the masses, political freedom must include real economic freedom of the starving millions."*
* **Question 2.1.2:** Under `[📜 Article 394](/atlas/art_394)` (PDF p. 282), which of the following provisions came into force **immediately on 26 November 1949** rather than waiting until 26 January 1950?
  * **A.** Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles).
  * **B.** **Citizenship (Articles 5–9), the Election Commission (Article 324), Presidential Oath (Article 60), and provisional/transitional provisions (Articles 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391–394).** *(Correct)*
  * **C.** Article 368 (Amendment of the Constitution).
  * **D.** The Seventh Schedule.
  * **Explained Rationale:** Article 394 explicitly lists the 16 articles (including Article 394 itself) that came into force "at once" on 26 November 1949 so citizenship rolls and the transitional institutional bridge could function prior to 26 January 1950.

lessons.title: Architectural Map of the 2026 Constitution: Internal Reorganization of States (Arts. 1–4) & Citizenship (Arts. 5–11)
lessons.levelTitle: Constitutional Structure, Fundamental Rights, DPSPs & Fundamental Duties

sections.title: 1. Lesson Title & Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
* **Title:** Architectural Map of the 2026 Constitution: Parts, Schedules, Internal Reorganization of States (Articles 1–4), and Constitutional Citizenship (Articles 5–11)

* **Measurable Learning Outcomes:**
  1. Navigate the complete structural map of the 2026 Constitution (**Preamble, 25 Parts, 470 extracted Articles, 12 Schedules, and 3 Appendices**).
  2. Analyze why Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described India under `[📜 Articles 1 to 4](/atlas/art_1)` as **"an indestructible Union of destructible States"**, contrasting `[📜 Article 2](/atlas/art_2)` (admission/establishment of new states) with `[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)` (internal reorganization, boundary changes, and renaming of existing states) and `[📜 Article 4](/atlas/art_4)` (why laws under Arts. 2 & 3 do NOT require an Article 368 Constitutional Amendment, except when ceding territory to a foreign nation per *Berubari Union* 1960 and the 100th Amendment `appendix_1`).
  3. Explain the constitutional design of `[📜 Part II Citizenship (Articles 5–11)](/atlas/part_II)`—distinguishing constitutional commencement citizenship (26 Jan 1950) from Parliament's plenary statutory power under `[📜 Article 11](/atlas/art_11)` (Citizenship Act, 1955) and distinguishing Fundamental Rights available **only to citizens** (`Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30`) from those available to **all persons** (`Arts. 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25–28`).

sections.title: 3. Compelling Opening Question / Real-World Problem
sections.text:
> **Two Border Changes — Why Did One Need a Simple Majority and the Other the 100th Constitutional Amendment?**  
> *Event A (June 2014):* Parliament enacted the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, carving out the new State of Telangana from Andhra Pradesh. Even though the Andhra Pradesh State Legislative Assembly passed a resolution *opposing* the bifurcation, Parliament passed the Act by a **simple majority** like an ordinary law!  
> *Event B (May 2015):* One year later, India and Bangladesh agreed to exchange 111 Indian enclaves in Bangladesh for 51 Bangladeshi enclaves in India to settle their border. This time, the Supreme Court's precedent said an ordinary law under Article 3 was **not enough**—Parliament had to pass the **100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 (`[📜 Appendix I](/atlas/appendix_1)`, PDF p. 382)** under `[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)`!  
> **The Question:** Why can Parliament redraw the map of any Indian State by a simple majority under `[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)` and `[📜 Article 4](/atlas/art_4)` even if the State Legislature objects—yet cannot cede a single square kilometre of Indian territory to a foreign country without an `[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)` Constitutional Amendment?

sections.title: 4. Beginner-Friendly Foundation (Before Advanced Terminology)
sections.text:
Think of the Republic of India as a large family home (`The Union`), and the 28 States (`Uttar Pradesh`, `Maharashtra`, `Tamil Nadu`, `Telangana`, etc.) as the rooms inside that home:
* **Moving an Interior Partition Wall (`[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)`):** If the family decides to divide one large bedroom into two bedrooms (like dividing Bihar into Bihar and Jharkhand in 2000, or Andhra Pradesh into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in 2014), the outer boundary of the house has not shrunk by a single inch. Under `[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)` and `[📜 Article 4(2)](/atlas/art_4)`, Parliament can rearrange these internal state boundaries by a **simple majority** after consulting the State Legislature (whose view is advisory, not binding!).
* **Giving Away Part of the Plot to a Neighbour (`[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)` & *Berubari Union* 1960):** If you want to transfer a piece of your plot to the neighbour next door (a foreign country), that is not an internal room rearrangement—it diminishes `[📜 Article 1](/atlas/art_1)` and the `[📜 First Schedule](/atlas/sched_1)`, which requires a full Constitutional Amendment under `[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)`.

sections.title: 5. Detailed Teachable Sections
sections.text:
#### Section 5.1: How Article 3 & Article 4 Work — Step-by-Step Procedure for State Reorganization In the United States, Article IV Section 3 of the US Constitution forbids Congress from forming a new State within an existing State without the **consent** of that State's legislature ("an indestructible Union of indestructible States"). Why did India reject the American rule in `[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)` (PDF pp. 33–34)? Because in 1949, British Indian provinces were administrative accidents of colonial conquest, and 552 Princely States had just been integrated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon. The framers knew India would need to reorganize its internal map along linguistic and administrative lines (as done by the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** and the **7th Amendment**). Under the **Proviso to Article 3** (substituted by the 5th Amendment Act, 1955, PDF p. 33–34), any Bill to form a new State or alter boundaries/names under Article 3 must follow two procedural safeguards: 1. **Prior Presidential Recommendation:** The Bill cannot be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the **recommendation of the President**. 2. **Presidential Reference to the State Legislature (For Views Within a Fixed Time):** If the Bill affects the area, boundaries, or name of any of the States, the President must refer the Bill to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views within such period as may be specified. * *Crucial Holding (*Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay*, `AIR 1960 SC 51`):* The President is bound to *refer* the Bill and wait for the specified period to expire, but **Parliament is NOT bound to accept the State Legislature's views**, nor does Parliament need to make a fresh reference if it amends the Bill during passage! * *Note on Union Territories (`Explanation I` to Art. 3 & *In Re: Article 370*, `2023 INSC 1058`):* For a Union Territory, the proviso does not even require a reference to the UT legislature, and under Explanation I (inserted by the 18th Amendment, 1966), "State" in clauses (a)–(e) of Article 3 includes a Union Territory. And look at `[📜 Article 4(1)–(2)](/atlas/art_4)` (PDF p. 34): * Any law made under Article 2 or Article 3 shall contain consequential amendments to the **First Schedule** (names/territories of States) and the **Fourth Schedule** (Rajya Sabha seat allocation). * **Article 4(2) explicitly declares:** *"No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368."* Hence, a **Simple Majority** suffices! * **The *Berubari Union* Qualification (`AIR 1960 SC 845`):** In *In Re: The Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves* (1960), the Supreme Court held that Article 3(c) ("diminish the area of any State") applies only to internal adjustments within the Union; it does **not** empower Parliament to cede Indian territory to a foreign state. Ceding territory requires an `[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)` amendment (which is why the 9th Amendment 1960 and the **100th Amendment Act, 2015** in `[📜 Appendix I](/atlas/appendix_1)`, PDF p. 382 were enacted), whereas merely settling a bona fide boundary dispute without ceding established territory can be done by executive action (*Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India*, 1969). #### Section 5.2: Part II Citizenship (`Articles 5–11`) & Citizens vs. All Persons in Part III `[STATUTORY_LAW]` India has **Single Constitutional Citizenship** (`[📜 Part II](/atlas/part_II)`, PDF pp. 35–36)—unlike the United States, there is no separate state citizenship, ensuring that every Indian citizen enjoys uniform rights of movement, residence, and public employment across the country (`[📜 Article 19(1)(d)–(e)](/atlas/art_19)`, `[📜 Article 16(1)–(2)](/atlas/art_16)`). * **Articles 5 to 8:** Define who became a citizen **at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950)**: * `Art. 5`: Citizenship by domicile in India. * `Art. 6`: Rights of citizenship of persons who migrated to India from Pakistan (before vs. on/after 19 July 1948, when the permit system was introduced). * `Art. 7`: Migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 (with proviso for those returning under a permit for resettlement or permanent return). * `Art. 8`: Persons of Indian origin residing outside India registering at Indian diplomatic missions. * **Article 9:** No person shall be a citizen under Arts. 5, 6, or 8 if they voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State. * **Article 10 & Article 11 (Plenary Power of Parliament):** `[📜 Article 11](/atlas/art_11)` (PDF p. 36) empowers Parliament to make any provision with respect to the **acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship** after 26 January 1950—exercised through the **Citizenship Act, 1955** (five statutory modes of acquisition: *Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalisation, and Incorporation of Territory*). **Essential Constitutional Table — Which Fundamental Rights Belong Only to Citizens vs. All Persons?** | Category | Constitutional Articles (Part III, PDF pp. 37–51) | Why This Distinction Exists | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Exclusive to Citizens of India Only** | • **`[📜 Article 15](/atlas/art_15)`** (Prohibition of discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth)
• **`[📜 Article 16](/atlas/art_16)`** (Equality of opportunity in public employment)
• **`[📜 Article 19](/atlas/art_19)`** (Six democratic freedoms: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession)
• **`[📜 Article 29](/atlas/art_29)` & `[📜 Article 30](/atlas/art_30)`** (Cultural and educational rights of minorities) *(plus voting under Art. 326 and holding high offices like President, VP, SC/HC Judge, Governor, AG)* | Political membership, unrestricted territorial movement/residence (`Art. 19(1)(d)–(e)`), and state service (`Art. 16`) are incidents of civic membership in the Republic. | | **Available to ALL Persons (Citizens & Non-Citizens / Foreigners)** | • **`[📜 Article 14](/atlas/art_14)`** (Equality before law and equal protection of laws)
• **`[📜 Article 20](/atlas/art_20)`** (Protection in respect of conviction for offences)
• **`[📜 Article 21](/atlas/art_21)`** (Protection of life and personal liberty)
• **`[📜 Article 21A](/atlas/art_21A)`** (Right to education for ages 6–14)
• **`[📜 Article 22](/atlas/art_22)`** (Protection against arrest and detention, except enemy aliens under Art. 22(3)(a))
• **`[📜 Articles 23–24](/atlas/art_23)`** (Against exploitation) & **`[📜 Articles 25–28](/atlas/art_25)`** (Freedom of religion) | Universal human rights grounded in basic human dignity and the Rule of Law apply to every human being within Indian jurisdiction (*Louis De Raedt v. Union of India*, 1991; *Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das*, 2000). |

sections.title: 6. Historical, Philosophical & Institutional Context
sections.text: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar stated on **12 August 1949** during the Constituent Assembly debate on Draft Articles 5 and 6 (CAD Vol. IX, p. 347): *"Except one or two articles, I do not think that any other article has given the Drafting Committee such a headache as this particular article."* Because Partition had displaced over 14 million people across the Punjab and Bengal borders, Articles 5–8 had to be crafted with surgical precision, while `[📜 Article 11](/atlas/art_11)` delegated permanent citizenship legislation to the future democratic Parliament.

sections.title: 7. Everyday Indian Civic Examples & Analogies
sections.text: * **A Foreign Tourist or Refugee and Article 21 vs. Article 19:** In *Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das* (`(2000) 2 SCC 465`), when a Bangladeshi national was assaulted by railway employees at Howrah Station, the Railway Board argued that as a foreign citizen she could not claim Fundamental Rights compensation. The Supreme Court rejected that defence and awarded compensation under `[📜 Article 21](/atlas/art_21)`, holding that Article 21 uses the word **"person"**, not "citizen", and protects every human being on Indian soil! Conversely, in *Louis De Raedt v. Union of India* (`(1991) 3 SCC 554`), the Court held that a foreign national cannot claim the right to reside and settle in India indefinitely, because that right belongs under `[📜 Article 19(1)(e)](/atlas/art_19)`, which applies **only to citizens**.

sections.title: 8. Verbatim Constitutional Articles & Primary Sources
10. Common Misconceptions & Their Corrections
sections.text:
* **Misconception:** *"If Parliament wants to change the name of a State (e.g., Orissa to Odisha) or create a new State out of an existing State, it needs a 2/3rds special majority under Article 368 and the consent of that State's Legislative Assembly."*
  * **Correction (constitutional text & judicial holding):** Under `[📜 Article 3](/atlas/art_3)` and `[📜 Article 4(2)](/atlas/art_4)` (PDF pp. 33–34), only a **Simple Majority** is required, and while the President must refer the Bill to the State Legislature for its views within a specified timeframe, **Parliament is not bound by the State Legislature's consent** (*Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay*, 1960).

sections.title: 12. Questions Requiring Active Reasoning
sections.text:
1. Why does `[📜 Article 4(1)](/atlas/art_4)` state that a law reorganizing states under Article 2 or Article 3 must amend **both** the `[📜 First Schedule](/atlas/sched_1)` and the `[📜 Fourth Schedule](/atlas/sched_4)`? Why would creating a new State automatically affect the Fourth Schedule?
2. Suppose a foreign company incorporated in Singapore or a foreign national visiting Mumbai challenges an arbitrary tax assessment order and a police search without warrant. Which Fundamental Rights in Part III can the foreign national invoke, and why can a company or foreigner NOT directly invoke `[📜 Article 19(1)(g)](/atlas/art_19)`?

sections.title: 13. Knowledge-Check Assessments with Explained Answers
sections.text:
* **Question 3.1.1:** Which of the following sets of Fundamental Rights is available **ONLY to citizens of India** and NOT to foreigners?
  * **A.** Articles 14, 20, 21, 25, and 27.
  * **B.** **Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30.** *(Correct)*
  * **C.** Articles 14, 19, 21, and 22.
  * **D.** Articles 17, 21A, 23, and 24.
  * **Explained Rationale:** Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 explicitly use the word **"citizen"** or **"citizens"**, whereas Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23–24, and 25–28 apply to any **"person"**.

sections.title: 14. Suggested Spaced-Review Questions (FSRS Flashcards)
sections.text:
1. **Card `fc_03_01_01`:** *Front:* Which five Fundamental Rights in Part III are guaranteed **exclusively to citizens** of India? → *Back:* **Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30.**
2. **Card `fc_03_01_02`:** *Front:* Under *In Re: Berubari Union* (1960), why was `[📜 Article 3(c)](/atlas/art_3)` held insufficient to transfer territory to Pakistan/Bangladesh? → *Back:* Because Article 3(c) only covers internal adjustments of state areas within the Union; ceding sovereign territory to a foreign state requires a Constitutional Amendment under `[📜 Article 368](/atlas/art_368)` (as done in the 9th Amendment 1960 and 100th Amendment 2015 `appendix_1`).

lessons.title: The Charter of Enforceable Liberties: Part III (Arts. 12–35), the Golden Triangle, Reasonable Restrictions & Art. 32
lessons.levelTitle: Constitutional Structure, Fundamental Rights, DPSPs & Fundamental Duties

sections.title: 1. Lesson Title & Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
* **Title:** The Charter of Enforceable Liberties: Part III (Articles 12–35), the Golden Triangle, Reasonable Restrictions, and the Heart and Soul of the Constitution (Article 32)

* **Measurable Learning Outcomes:**
  1. Apply both tests under `[📜 Article 14](/atlas/art_14)`: (a) the **Traditional Reasonable Classification Test** (*intelligible differentia* + *rational nexus*, *Anwar Ali Sarkar* 1952) and (b) the **New Non-Arbitrariness Test** (*E.P. Royappa* 1974, *Maneka Gandhi* 1978, and *Shayara Bano* 2017 "Manifest Arbitrariness").
  2. Map each of the **six democratic freedoms** in `[📜 Article 19(1)(a)–(g)](/atlas/art_19)` to its **exhaustive permissible grounds of reasonable restriction** in Clauses `19(2)` through `19(6)`, explaining why a restriction on free speech (`19(1)(a)`) cannot be justified on "general public interest" (`19(6)`) if it does not fall within the eight specific grounds of `Article 19(2)` (*Sakal Papers* 1962; *Shreya Singhal* `judg_shreya_singhal` 2015).
  3. Analyze the criminal-justice and personal-liberty guarantees of `[📜 Article 20](/atlas/art_20)` (ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination), `[📜 Article 21](/atlas/art_21)` (life, dignity, privacy `phil_privacy`, livelihood `judg_olga_tellis`), `[📜 Article 21A](/atlas/art_21A)` (education), and `[📜 Article 22](/atlas/art_22)` (arrest safeguards `judg_dk_basu` vs. preventive detention limits).
  4. Compare the scope of `[📜 Article 32](/atlas/art_32)` (Supreme Court writ jurisdiction, itself a Fundamental Right) with `[📜 Article 226](/atlas/art_226)` (High Court writ jurisdiction).

sections.title: 3. Compelling Opening Question / Real-World Problem
sections.text:
> **Can a Government Restrict Newspaper Pages in the Name of "Public Interest"?**  
> In 1960, the Central Government passed an order fixing the maximum number of pages a newspaper could publish at a given price. When the newspaper *Sakal* challenged this order as a violation of **Freedom of Speech and Expression (`[📜 Article 19(1)(a)](/atlas/art_19)`)**, the Government argued: *"We are regulating the business of newspapers in the 'interest of the general public', which is an explicitly permitted restriction under Article 19(6)!"*  
> **The Question:** Why did the Supreme Court in *Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India* (`AIR 1962 SC 305`) strike down the order? Why can the State use **"in the interests of the general public"** to restrict a trade or business under `Article 19(6)`, yet is **strictly forbidden** from using "in the interests of the general public" to restrict Freedom of Speech and Expression under `Article 19(2)`?

sections.title: 4. Beginner-Friendly Foundation (Before Advanced Terminology)
sections.text:
Think of `[📜 Part III (Articles 12 to 35)](/atlas/part_III)` as six interlocking shields protecting every citizen's freedom and dignity, backed by a sword (`[📜 Article 32](/atlas/art_32)`) to enforce them:
1. **Right to Equality (`[📜 Articles 14–18](/atlas/art_14)`):** Equal treatment by law, no discrimination on religion/race/caste/sex/birthplace (`Art. 15`), equal public job opportunity (`Art. 16`), abolition of untouchability (`Art. 17`), and abolition of colonial titles (`Art. 18`).
2. **Right to Freedom (`[📜 Articles 19–22](/atlas/art_19)`):** Six democratic freedoms (`Art. 19`), criminal-trial protections (`Art. 20`), right to life, dignity, privacy, and fair procedure (`Art. 21`), right to education (`Art. 21A`), and safeguards on arrest (`Art. 22`).
3. **Right Against Exploitation (`[📜 Articles 23–24](/atlas/art_23)`):** Prohibition of human trafficking, *begar* (forced labour), and child labour under age 14 in hazardous employments.
4. **Right to Freedom of Religion (`[📜 Articles 25–28](/atlas/art_25)`):** Freedom of conscience and right freely to profess, practice, and propagate religion (`Art. 25`), manage religious affairs (`Art. 26`), no tax for promoting any particular religion (`Art. 27`), and no compulsory religious instruction in state-funded schools (`Art. 28`).
5. **Cultural and Educational Rights (`[📜 Articles 29–30](/atlas/art_29)`):** Protection of distinct language, script, or culture (`Art. 29`) and right of religious and linguistic minorities to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice (`Art. 30`).
6. **Right to Constitutional Remedies (`[📜 Articles 32–35](/atlas/art_32)`):** Guaranteed right to move the `[🏛️ Supreme Court](/atlas/inst_supreme_court)` directly for the enforcement of Part III rights via the five prerogative writs—which Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called *"the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it"* (CAD Vol. VII, 9 Dec 1948, p. 953).

sections.title: 5. Detailed Teachable Sections
sections.text:
#### Section 5.1: The Precision Matrix of Article 19(1) Freedoms vs. Clauses 19(2)–19(6) Restrictions
In `[📜 Article 19](/atlas/art_19)` (Official 2026 PDF, pp. 40–41), the framers did not leave the permissible limits on citizen freedoms vague. Each of the six freedoms in `Article 19(1)` has its own **dedicated, closed-list restriction clause**:

| Freedom in Article 19(1) | Controlling Restriction Clause | Exhaustive Permissible Grounds for "Reasonable Restrictions" by Law |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`19(1)(a)` Freedom of speech and expression** *(includes press, right to know, commercial speech, internet access)* | **`Article 19(2)`** *(Amended by 1st & 16th Amendments)* | **8 Grounds ONLY:** (1) Sovereignty and integrity of India, (2) Security of the State, (3) Friendly relations with foreign States, (4) Public order, (5) Decency or morality, (6) Contempt of court, (7) Defamation, or (8) Incitement to an offence. *(Note: "Interests of the general public" is NOT a ground under 19(2)!)* |
| **`19(1)(b)` Assemble peaceably and without arms** | **`Article 19(3)`** | **2 Grounds ONLY:** (1) Sovereignty and integrity of India, or (2) Public order. |
| **`19(1)(c)` Form associations or unions [or co-operative societies — 97th Amend.]** | **`Article 19(4)`** | **3 Grounds ONLY:** (1) Sovereignty and integrity of India, (2) Public order, or (3) Morality. |
| **`19(1)(d)` Move freely throughout the territory of India** & **`19(1)(e)` Reside and settle in any part of India** *(Note: 19(1)(f) Property omitted by 44th Amend. 1978)* | **`Article 19(5)`** | **2 Grounds ONLY:** (1) In the interests of the general public, or (2) For the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe. |
| **`19(1)(g)` Practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business** | **`Article 19(6)`** | **Interests of the general public**, PLUS (i) prescribing professional or technical qualifications, and (ii) State monopoly in any trade/business/industry (`1st Amendment, 1951`). |

In `[⚖️ Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)](/atlas/judg_shreya_singhal)` (`(2015) 5 SCC 1`), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (which criminalized sending "offensive" or "annoying" messages online) because mere annoyance or inconvenience does not amount to **"public order"** or **"incitement to an offence"** under `Article 19(2)`, drawing a crystal-clear constitutional line between protected **discussion and advocacy** (however unpopular) and unprotected **incitement to imminent lawless action**.

#### Section 5.2: Articles 20, 21, 21A, and 22 — The Criminal Justice & Personal Liberty Shield
1. **`[📜 Article 20](/atlas/art_20)` (Three Non-Derogable Criminal Protections, PDF p. 41):**
   * **Clause 20(1) — Protection Against *Ex Post Facto* Criminal Laws:** No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force *at the time of the commission of the act*, nor subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at that time. *(Note: Applies to substantive criminal laws, not retrospective civil or tax laws, though retrospective beneficial reductions in criminal punishment are permitted per Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab, 1965).*
   * **Clause 20(2) — Protection Against Double Jeopardy (*Nemo debet bis vexari*):** No person shall be prosecuted **and** punished for the same offence more than once (requires prior judicial prosecution + punishment; departmental inquiry followed by criminal trial does not violate 20(2), *Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay*, 1953).
   * **Clause 20(3) — Protection Against Self-Incrimination:** No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (bars involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping tests without consent per *Selvi v. State of Karnataka*, `(2010) 7 SCC 263`).
2. **`[📜 Article 21](/atlas/art_21)` & The Golden Triangle (`[⚖️ Maneka Gandhi](/atlas/judg_maneka)`, `[⚖️ Puttaswamy](/atlas/judg_puttaswamy)`):**
   * Originally in `[⚖️ A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)](/atlas/judg_gopalan)`, the majority held that "procedure established by law" meant any statutory procedure enacted by Parliament, and treated Articles 19, 21, and 22 as water-tight compartments.
   * In `[⚖️ Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)](/atlas/judg_maneka)`, a 7-Judge Bench overruled *Gopalan*, holding that Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an integrated `[⚖️ Golden Triangle](/atlas/doc_golden_triangle)` and that any procedure depriving life or personal liberty under Article 21 must be **"right and just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive."**
   * Through `[⚖️ Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)](/atlas/judg_puttaswamy)` (9-Judge Bench), the Court affirmed `[🏛️ Right to Privacy](/atlas/phil_privacy)` as an intrinsic facet of Article 21 and Part III, governed by the 4-prong `[⚖️ Proportionality Test](/atlas/doc_proportionality)`.
   * Crucially, under `[📜 Article 359(1)](/atlas/art_359)` (as amended by the `[📜 44th Amendment Act, 1978](/atlas/amend_44)`), the enforcement of **Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended even during a National Emergency**!
3. **`[📜 Article 22](/atlas/art_22)` (Ordinary Arrest vs. Preventive Detention, PDF pp. 41–42):**
   * **Clauses 22(1)–(2) (Punitive Arrest Safeguards):** Every arrested person has the right to (i) be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of arrest, (ii) consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of their choice, and (iii) **be produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest** (excluding journey time), and cannot be detained beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's authority (reinforced by `[⚖️ D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)](/atlas/judg_dk_basu)`).
   * **Clauses 22(4)–(7) (Constitutional Limits on Preventive Detention):** Under Clause 22(3), clauses (1) and (2) do not apply to enemy aliens or persons arrested under a preventive detention law, **but** Clauses 22(4)–(5) mandate that no preventive detention law can authorize detention beyond **three months** unless an Advisory Board (consisting of sitting or qualified High Court Judges) reports before the expiration of those three months that there is sufficient cause, and the detenu must be communicated the grounds as soon as may be and afforded the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order.

sections.title: 6. Historical, Philosophical & Institutional Context
sections.text: When Draft Article 15 (`[📜 Article 21](/atlas/art_21)`) was debated on 6 and 13 December 1948, why did the Drafting Committee drop the American phrase *"without due process of law"*? During his 1947 visit to Washington, Constitutional Adviser **Sir B.N. Rau** met U.S. Supreme Court Justice **Felix Frankfurter**, who warned Rau that in the *Lochner* era (1905–1937), conservative U.S. judges had used "substantive due process" to strike down minimum-wage and social-welfare laws! However, many Assembly members (including K.M. Munshi, Thakur Das Bhargava, and Chimanlal Chitaley) feared that removing "due process" would leave personal liberty vulnerable to arbitrary police arrest. To resolve that exact fear, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar introduced Draft Article 15A (`[📜 Article 22](/atlas/art_22)`) on 15 September 1949 (CAD Vol. IX, p. 1497) to write explicit 24-hour magistrate production and legal-counsel guarantees directly into the text, and 28 years later `[⚖️ Maneka Gandhi (1978)](/atlas/judg_maneka)` synthesized procedural and substantive fairness into Article 21!

sections.title: 7. Everyday Indian Civic Examples & Analogies
sections.text: * **What Happens When Police Arrest a Citizen on Friday Night (`Article 22(2)` & `D.K. Basu`):** Suppose a citizen is arrested at 8:00 PM on Friday. Can the Station House Officer (SHO) say, *"Saturday and Sunday are court holidays, so I will keep him in the police lock-up until Monday morning"*? **Absolutely not!** `[📜 Article 22(2)](/atlas/art_22)` (PDF p. 42) is an absolute constitutional command: the arrested person MUST be produced before the nearest Judicial Magistrate (who holds holiday/duty remand rosters in every Indian district) **within 24 hours** (by 8:00 PM Saturday, excluding travel time), failing which the detention becomes unconstitutional and amenable to a **Writ of Habeas Corpus** under `[📜 Article 226](/atlas/art_226)` or `[📜 Article 32](/atlas/art_32)`.

sections.title: 8. Verbatim Constitutional Articles & Primary Sources
sections.text:
* **Article 21A, Part III — Inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 (Official 2026 PDF, p. 41):**
  > **21A. Right to education.—**The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.
* **Article 22(1)–(2), Part III (Official 2026 PDF, pp. 41–42):**
  > **22. Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases.—**(1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.  
  > (2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.
* **Article 32(1)–(2), Part III (Official 2026 PDF, p. 45):**
  > **32. Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part.—**(1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.  
  > (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of *habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto* and *certiorari*, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.

sections.title: 10. Common Misconceptions & Their Corrections
sections.text:
* **Misconception:** *"Because the Supreme Court is higher than a High Court, the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is wider in scope than a High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226."*
  * **Correction (constitutional text):** Territorially, the Supreme Court's writ runs across all of India, **but in terms of subject-matter scope, a High Court's writ jurisdiction under `[📜 Article 226](/atlas/art_226)` (PDF p. 137) is WIDER than `[📜 Article 32](/atlas/art_32)`**! Why? Because Article 32 can be invoked **only** for the enforcement of **Part III Fundamental Rights**, whereas Article 226 empowers a High Court to issue writs both for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights **"and for any other purpose"** (such as enforcing ordinary statutory rights, challenging administrative ultra vires, or enforcing Article 300A property rights). At the same time, Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right (so the Supreme Court cannot refuse to entertain a bona fide Part III violation, *Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras*, 1950), whereas relief under Article 226 for non-fundamental rights is discretionary.

sections.title: 12. Questions Requiring Active Reasoning
sections.text:
1. Trace the doctrinal journey from `[⚖️ A.K. Gopalan (1950)](/atlas/judg_gopalan)` to `[⚖️ Maneka Gandhi (1978)](/atlas/judg_maneka)` and `[⚖️ Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)](/atlas/judg_puttaswamy)`. How did the overruling of *Gopalan*'s "silo theory" change the way courts evaluate any law that touches personal liberty?
2. Why did the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 (`[📜 86th Amendment](/atlas/amend_86)`) simultaneously amend **three different Parts** of the Constitution—inserting `[📜 Article 21A](/atlas/art_21A)` in Part III, substituting `[📜 Article 45](/atlas/art_45)` in Part IV, and adding clause `(k)` to `[📜 Article 51A](/atlas/art_51A)` in Part IVA?

sections.title: 13. Knowledge-Check Assessments with Explained Answers
sections.text:
* **Question 3.2.1:** Which of the following is **NOT** one of the eight permissible grounds for imposing reasonable restrictions on the Freedom of Speech and Expression under `[📜 Article 19(2)](/atlas/art_19)`?
  * **A.** Public order.
  * **B.** Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  * **C.** **In the interests of the general public.** *(Correct)*
  * **D.** Incitement to an offence.
  * **Explained Rationale:** Under Article 19(2) (PDF p. 40), "in the interests of the general public" is deliberately omitted (whereas it is present in Articles 19(5) and 19(6)), so the State cannot restrict speech merely by claiming a general public-interest rationale (*Sakal Papers*, 1962; *Shreya Singhal*, 2015).
* **Question 3.2.2:** Under `[📜 Article 359(1)](/atlas/art_359)` of the Constitution (as amended by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978), the enforcement of which two Fundamental Rights can **NEVER** be suspended by Presidential Order even during a Proclamation of National Emergency?
  * **A.** Articles 14 and 19.
  * **B.** **Articles 20 and 21.** *(Correct)*
  * **C.** Articles 19 and 21.
  * **D.** Articles 25 and 32.
  * **Explained Rationale:** Enacted after the grave experience of *ADM Jabalpur* (1976), the `[📜 44th Amendment Act, 1978](/atlas/amend_44)` amended `[📜 Article 359(1)](/atlas/art_359)` (PDF p. 244) to add the parenthetical protection `(except articles 20 and 21)`, ensuring that the right to life, personal liberty, and criminal-trial safeguards remain enforceable in court even during war or emergency.

lessons.title: The Conscience of the Constitution: Directive Principles (Part IV), Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) & Harmonious Construction
lessons.levelTitle: Constitutional Structure, Fundamental Rights, DPSPs & Fundamental Duties

sections.title: 1. Lesson Title & Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
* **Title:** The Conscience of the Constitution: Directive Principles (Articles 36–51), Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), and *Minerva Mills* Harmonious Construction

* **Measurable Learning Outcomes:**
  1. Explain the dual mandate of `[📜 Article 37](/atlas/art_37)` (PDF p. 52): why Directive Principles in `[📜 Part IV](/atlas/part_IV)` are *"not enforceable by any court"*, yet are *"nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws."*
  2. Categorize the Directive Principles across their three intellectual traditions (**Socialistic & Welfare Directives** `Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47`; **Gandhian Directives** `Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48`; and **Liberal-Intellectual Directives** `Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51`) and trace how Constitutional Amendments (`42nd`, `44th`, `86th`, `97th`) expanded Part IV.
  3. Trace the constitutional conflict and reconciliation between Part III and Part IV from *Champakam Dorairajan* (1951) and *Kerala Education Bill* (1957) through `[📜 Article 31C](/atlas/art_31C)` (25th & 42nd Amendments) to the landmark holding in `[⚖️ Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)](/atlas/judg_minerva)` establishing `[⚖️ Harmonious Construction](/atlas/doc_harmonious_const)`.
  4. Analyze the 11 **Fundamental Duties** under `[📜 Article 51A](/atlas/art_51A)` (`[📜 Part IVA](/atlas/part_IVA)`, PDF p. 55) and how courts use both Part IV and Part IVA to determine the "reasonableness" of statutory restrictions under Articles 14, 19, and 21.

sections.title: 3. Compelling Opening Question / Real-World Problem
sections.text:
> **Are Directive Principles Just "Pious Wishes" — Or Can They Save a Law from Being Struck Down?**  
> In 1948, a member of the Constituent Assembly (Naziruddin Ahmad) mocked Part IV as *"a set of pious resolution—like a New Year's resolution broken on the second of January"* because `[📜 Article 37](/atlas/art_37)` says no court can directly enforce them.  
> Yet fifty years later, when slaughterhouse owners challenged a complete statutory ban on slaughtering draught cattle in Gujarat as an unreasonable restriction on their right to carry on a trade under `[📜 Article 19(1)(g)](/atlas/art_19)`, a 7-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in *State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat* (`(2005) 8 SCC 534`) **upheld the ban** by pointing directly to `[📜 Article 48](/atlas/art_48)` (Directive Principle on agriculture and animal husbandry), `[📜 Article 48A](/atlas/art_48A)` (environment), and `[📜 Article 51A(g)](/atlas/art_51A)` (Fundamental Duty to have compassion for living creatures)!  
> **The Question:** If Part IV and Part IVA cannot be directly enforced by a writ of mandamus, how do they nevertheless wield immense legal power in court—and why did the Supreme Court in `[⚖️ Minerva Mills (1980)](/atlas/judg_minerva)` strike down an amendment that tried to make Part IV completely override Part III?

sections.title: 4. Beginner-Friendly Foundation (Before Advanced Terminology)
sections.text:
In `[⚖️ Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)](/atlas/judg_minerva)`, Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud used a famous metaphor: **Fundamental Rights (`[📜 Part III](/atlas/part_III)`) and Directive Principles (`[📜 Part IV](/atlas/part_IV)`) are like the two wheels of a chariot.**
* **Part III (Fundamental Rights)** tells the State **what it must NOT do** (the constitutional brakes and steering rules protecting individual freedom).
* **Part IV (Directive Principles)** tells the State **where the chariot must go** (the destination of social and economic democracy—living wages, equal pay for equal work, village panchayats, environmental protection, free legal aid).
* If you remove one wheel—either by sacrificing individual freedom in the name of welfare, or by blocking all social-welfare legislation in the name of absolute property/contract rights—the chariot of Indian democracy crashes!

sections.title: 5. Detailed Teachable Sections
sections.text:
#### Section 5.1: Dr. Ambedkar's Conception of Directives as "Instruments of Instructions" & Political Accountability
Why did the framers call Part IV "Directive Principles"? Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explained on **4 November 1948** (CAD Vol. VII, p. 41) that Directive Principles are like the **Instruments of Instructions** issued to the Governor-General and Governors under the 1935 Act—with one crucial difference: instead of being instructions from the British Crown to colonial governors, **Part IV is a binding constitutional instruction from the sovereign People of India to every future Legislature and Executive** at the Union, State, and Local levels (`[📜 Article 36](/atlas/art_36)` incorporates `[📜 Article 12](/atlas/art_12)`'s broad definition of "the State").

Dr. Ambedkar added a famous warning:
> *"Whoever captures power will not be free to do what he likes with it. In the exercise of it, he will have to respect these Instruments of Instructions which are called Directive Principles. He cannot ignore them. He may not have to answer for their breach in a Court of Law. But he will certainly have to answer for them before the electorate at election time."*

#### Section 5.2: Complete Classification of Part IV (`Articles 36–51`) & Major Statutory Implementations
`[STATUTORY_LAW]`  
Far from remaining "pious wishes," Part IV has served as the legislative blueprint for hundreds of landmark Parliamentary and State statutes over the last 75 years:

| Directive Principle (Official 2026 PDF, pp. 52–55) | Core Mandate | Major Statutory / Constitutional Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`[📜 Article 38](/atlas/art_38)`** *(Cl. 2 added by 44th Amend. 1978)* | Secure a social order informed by social, economic, and political justice; minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities | Welfare legislation, progressive taxation, affirmative action, NITI Aayog / planning |
| **`[📜 Article 39(a)–(f)](/atlas/art_39)`** *(Cl. (f) substituted by 42nd Amend. 1976)* | Adequate means of livelihood `(a)`; distribution of ownership and control of **material resources of the community** for the common good `(b)`; operation of economic system not resulting in **concentration of wealth and means of production** to common detriment `(c)`; **equal pay for equal work** for both men and women `(d)`; health/strength of workers and children `(e)–(f)` | Land Reform Acts, Nationalization Acts, Equal Remuneration Act 1976 / Code on Wages 2019, MGNREGA 2005, Competition Act 2002, POCSO Act |
| **`[📜 Article 39A](/atlas/art_39A)`** *(Inserted by 42nd Amend. 1976)* | **Equal justice and free legal aid** so opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities | **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (NALSA, SALSA, DALSA & Lok Adalats) |
| **`[📜 Article 40](/atlas/art_40)`** | **Organisation of village panchayats** and endowing them with powers to function as units of self-government | Constitutionalized by the **`[📜 73rd Amendment Act, 1992](/atlas/amend_73_74)`** (`[📜 Part IX](/atlas/part_IX)`, Arts. 243–243O) |
| **`[📜 Articles 41, 42, 43, 43A, 43B](/atlas/art_41)`** *(43A by 42nd Amend.; 43B by 97th Amend. 2011)* | Right to work, education, public assistance (`41`); just and humane conditions of work & **maternity relief** (`42`); living wage & cottage industries (`43`); participation of workers in management (`43A`); **co-operative societies** (`43B`) | Maternity Benefit Act 1961 (26 weeks paid leave), MGNREGA 2005, Labour Codes, Part IXB (`243ZH–243ZT`) |
| **`[📜 Article 44](/atlas/art_44)`** | Endeavour to secure for the citizens a **uniform civil code** throughout the territory of India | Codification of secular marriage/succession laws (Special Marriage Act 1954), Goa Civil Code, Uttarakhand UCC Act 2024 |
| **`[📜 Article 45](/atlas/art_45)`** *(Substituted by 86th Amend. 2002)* | Early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the **age of six years** (while ages 6–14 moved to `[📜 Article 21A](/atlas/art_21A)`) | Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS / Anganwadi) & Right to Education Act, 2009 |
| **`[📜 Articles 46, 47, 48, 48A](/atlas/art_48A)`** *(48A by 42nd Amend. 1976)* | Educational and economic interests of SCs/STs (`46`); nutrition, standard of living, and public health (`47`); agriculture & animal husbandry (`48`); **protection and improvement of environment, forests, and wild life** (`48A`) | National Food Security Act 2013, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Forest Conservation Act 1980 |
| **`[📜 Articles 49, 50, 51](/atlas/art_50)`** | Protection of monuments of national importance (`49`); **separation of judiciary from executive** (`50`); promotion of **international peace and security**, just and honourable relations between nations, respect for international law and treaty obligations (`51`) | Ancient Monuments Act 1958, CrPC 1973 / BNSS 2023 judicial separation, and `[⚖️ Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)](/atlas/judg_vishaka)` reading international conventions into domestic law via Art. 51(c) |

#### Section 5.3: The Constitutional Struggle Over Primacy (`Article 31C` & `Minerva Mills`)
Trace the four-stage doctrinal evolution between Part III and Part IV:
1. **Stage 1 — Strict Subordination (*Champakam Dorairajan*, 1951):** The Supreme Court initially stated that Directive Principles must "conform to and run as subsidiary to" the Chapter of Fundamental Rights.
2. **Stage 2 — Harmonious Construction Introduced (*In Re: The Kerala Education Bill*, 1957):** Chief Justice S.R. Das held that courts should not entirely ignore Part IV when interpreting Part III, but should adopt the **Principle of Harmonious Construction (`[⚖️ Harmonious Construction](/atlas/doc_harmonious_const)`)** to give effect to both as far as possible.
3. **Stage 3 — The 25th Amendment (1971) & *Kesavananda Bharati* (1973):** The 25th Amendment inserted `[📜 Article 31C](/atlas/art_31C)` (PDF p. 45), which provided that no law giving effect to the specific Socialist Directives in **`Article 39(b)` or `Article 39(c)`** (preventing concentration of wealth and distributing material resources for the common good) shall be deemed void on the ground that it violates `Article 14` or `Article 19`. In `[⚖️ Kesavananda Bharati (1973)](/atlas/judg_kesavananda)`, the 13-Judge Bench **upheld** this narrow protection for `Article 39(b)–(c)` (while striking down the second part of Art. 31C that had barred judicial review of whether the law actually gave effect to that policy).
4. **Stage 4 — The 42nd Amendment Overreach (1976) & *Minerva Mills* (1980):** Section 4 of the `[📜 42nd Amendment Act, 1976](/atlas/amend_42)` amended Article 31C to replace *"the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39"* with **"all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV"**—effectively subordinating Articles 14 and 19 to every single Directive Principle! In `[⚖️ Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)](/atlas/judg_minerva)` (`(1980) 3 SCC 625`), the Supreme Court **struck down Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment**, holding:
   > *"The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Parts III and IV. To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution. This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution."*  
   *(Note: Also note the recent 9-Judge Bench ruling in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, `2024 INSC 835`, confirming that the unamended text of Article 31C protecting genuine Article 39(b)–(c) laws remains in force after Minerva Mills, while clarifying that not every piece of private property automatically constitutes a "material resource of the community" under Article 39(b)).*

#### Section 5.4: Fundamental Duties (`Part IVA`, `Article 51A`)
The original 1950 Constitution did not contain a separate chapter of Fundamental Duties. Acting on the recommendations of the ** Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976)**, the `[📜 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976](/atlas/amend_42)` inserted `[📜 Part IVA (Article 51A)](/atlas/part_IVA)` (PDF pp. 55–56) specifying **10 Fundamental Duties** of every citizen of India, and the `[📜 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002](/atlas/amend_86)` added the **11th Duty (`Article 51A(k)`)** requiring a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the age of 6 and 14 years.

While Fundamental Duties (like DPSPs) are not directly enforceable by writs against private citizens without an enabling statute (such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 or Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, as noted by the **Justice J.S. Verma Committee Report, 1999**), the Supreme Court held in *AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS* (`(2002) 1 SCC 428`) that Fundamental Duties provide a valuable constitutional yardstick when testing the reasonableness of laws under Articles 14 and 19.

sections.title: 6. Historical, Philosophical & Institutional Context
sections.text: Granville Austin famously wrote that **Part III and Part IV together constitute "the Conscience of the Constitution"**—linking the **National Revolution** (political independence and civil liberties) with the **Social Revolution** (lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty, illiteracy, and caste subordination through democratic law).

sections.title: 7. Everyday Indian Civic Examples & Analogies
sections.text:
`[STATUTORY_LAW]`  
* **How You Can Walk Into Any District Court and Get a Free Lawyer (`[📜 Article 39A](/atlas/art_39A)` → DALSA):** If an indigent citizen in Ghaziabad or Patna cannot afford a lawyer for a civil or criminal case, they can walk into the **District Legal Services Authority (DALSA)** office in the District Court complex (chaired by the District & Sessions Judge under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, enacted to implement `[📜 Article 39A](/atlas/art_39A)`, PDF p. 53) and receive a court-appointed panel advocate and exemption from court fees at zero cost!

sections.title: 8. Verbatim Constitutional Articles & Primary Sources
sections.text:
* **Article 37, Part IV (Official 2026 Constitution PDF, p. 52):**
  > **37. Application of the principles contained in this Part.—**The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
* **Article 51A(a), (e), (g), (h), (k), Part IVA (Official 2026 Constitution PDF, pp. 55–56):**
  > **51A. Fundamental duties.—**It shall be the duty of every citizen of India—  
  > (a) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; ...  
  > (e) to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; ...  
  > (g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures;  
  > (h) to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; ...  
  > (k) who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.

sections.title: 10. Common Misconceptions & Their Corrections
sections.text:
* **Misconception:** *"Because Article 37 says Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, courts completely ignore Part IV when deciding constitutional cases."*
  * **Correction (judicial holding):** Courts cannot issue a writ forcing Parliament to enact a new law under Part IV, **but** courts constantly use Part IV in two powerful ways: (1) **reading Part III rights expansively** in light of Part IV (e.g., reading the right to livelihood into `Art. 21` via `Art. 39(a)` & `41` in `[⚖️ Olga Tellis](/atlas/judg_olga_tellis)`, free legal aid via `Art. 39A` in *Hussainara Khatoon*, and clean environment via `Art. 48A` in *M.C. Mehta*), and (2) **upholding statutory restrictions on Article 19 rights as "reasonable"** when the statute implements a Directive Principle!

sections.title: 12. Questions Requiring Active Reasoning
sections.text:
1. Why did the Supreme Court uphold `[📜 Article 31C](/atlas/art_31C)` to the extent it protected laws implementing **`Article 39(b)` and `Article 39(c)`** in `[⚖️ Kesavananda Bharati (1973)](/atlas/judg_kesavananda)`, yet strike down the 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C to **all of Part IV** in `[⚖️ Minerva Mills (1980)](/atlas/judg_minerva)`?
2. Notice that `[📜 Article 51A](/atlas/art_51A)` begins with *"It shall be the duty of every **citizen** of India"*. Why do Fundamental Duties apply only to citizens rather than to foreign visitors?

sections.title: 13. Knowledge-Check Assessments with Explained Answers
sections.text:
* **Question 3.3.1:** Which four Directive Principles were added or amended by the `[📜 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976](/atlas/amend_42)`?
  * **A.** Articles 40, 44, 45, and 50.
  * **B.** **Article 39(f) (healthy development of children), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries), and Article 48A (protection and improvement of environment, forests, and wild life).** *(Correct)*
  * **C.** Articles 38(2), 43B, 45, and 51.
  * **D.** Articles 36, 37, 47, and 49.
  * **Explained Rationale:** The 42nd Amendment (1976) substituted `Art. 39(f)` and inserted `Art. 39A`, `Art. 43A`, and `Art. 48A`. (`Art. 38(2)` was added by the 44th Amendment 1978, `Art. 45` was substituted by the 86th Amendment 2002, and `Art. 43B` was inserted by the 97th Amendment 2011).
